description: Test your knowledge of Features of individual bones (Lower Limb).

cards.text: What is the acetabulum and which three bones form the hip bone?
cards.answer: The acetabulum is a cup-shaped socket that articulates with the femoral head to form the hip joint. The hip bone (os coxae) is formed by fusion of the ilium (superior), ischium (posteroinferior), and pubis (anteroinferior).

tip.tip: IAP = Ilium-Ischium-Pubis; all three converge at the acetabulum

cards.text: Where is the ASIS and why is it clinically important?
cards.answer: The anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) is the palpable bony landmark at the anterior upper border of the ilium. It is the attachment for sartorius and the inguinal ligament, and serves as a key landmark in clinical examinations.

tip.tip: ASIS = your visible hip bone bump; palpate and use for surface anatomy

cards.text: Name the bony prominence you sit on and its anatomical attachments.
cards.answer: The ischial tuberosity is the bony bump you sit on. It is the origin of the hamstring muscles and is prone to pressure sores (decubitus ulcers) in bedridden patients.

tip.tip: Ischial tuberosity = your "sitting bone"; pressure sores develop here in immobile patients

cards.text: What is the clinical significance of the ischial spine?
cards.answer: The ischial spine is a landmark that divides the greater and lesser sciatic notches and is the target landmark for a pudendal nerve block in obstetrics (e.g., for pain relief during childbirth).

tip.tip: Ischial spine = pudendal nerve block site; used in obstetric anesthesia

cards.text: What does the fovea capitis of the femoral head contain and why is it clinically significant?
cards.answer: The fovea capitis (pit on the femoral head) is the attachment for the ligament of the head of femur, which carries the obturator artery. This is the only blood supply to the femoral head in adults and is critically compromised in intracapsular neck fractures, leading to avascular necrosis.

tip.tip: Fovea capitis = femoral head blood supply; intracapsular fractures → AVN risk

cards.text: What is the normal neck-shaft angle of the femur and what happens when it is reduced?
cards.answer: The normal neck-shaft angle is approximately 126° in adults. When reduced, the condition is called coxa vara; when increased, it is called coxa valga. The femoral neck is intracapsular, so fractures here risk avascular necrosis.

tip.tip: Normal = 126°; Less = coxa vara (varus = "turned in"); More = coxa valga

cards.text: How can the lower end of the femur be used radiologically to confirm term pregnancy?
cards.answer: The epiphysis of the lower end of femur appears at the 9th month of intrauterine life. Its presence on radiography indicates the fetus is ≥36 weeks gestation (term pregnancy).

tip.tip: Lower femoral epiphysis = 9th month IUL; confirms term pregnancy on X-ray

cards.text: Which muscles attach to the greater and lesser trochanters, and what are their functions?
cards.answer: The greater trochanter is the attachment for the gluteus medius and minimus (hip abductors). The lesser trochanter is the attachment for the iliopsoas (primary hip flexor).

tip.tip: Greater = Glute med/min (ABduct); Lesser = ilioPs (flexes); G before L in anatomy
